# W-004 — Counter peek (behavioral specification)

This is the only task statement the agent sees. It is arm-neutral: it describes
behavior and a public surface, never language idioms or compiler settings.

## Existing behavior (already implemented in the starting fixture)

`Counter` holds an *observer* — a step that receives an integer — and
`Bump(n)` hands `n` to the observer. As delivered the observer is never
installed, so the class is not yet usable; that is part of the task.

## Task: extend the class

1. Construction — a `Counter` built with its public parameterless constructor
   installs its observer: a step that **prints the value it receives on its own
   line**. The counter also starts a running total at `0`.
2. `Bump(n)` → nothing — adds `n` to the running total and hands the **new
   total** to the observer (so a fresh counter's `Bump(3)` prints `3`, and a
   following `Bump(4)` prints `7`).
3. `Peek(n)` → integer — returns the total that `Bump(n)` *would* produce
   (`total + n`) **without changing the total**: `Peek` is a pure read, it
   prints nothing.

## Constraints

- `Bump` prints exactly one line per call and nothing else.
- `Peek` prints nothing, on a fresh counter and on one that has been bumped;
  after `Peek(n)` the total is what it was before.
- Declare effects the way the existing code does.

## If the starter does not build as delivered

It does. Build first, then extend.

## Public surface (pinned; held-out tests bind to it via a fixed shim)

Class `Counter` with a public parameterless constructor and instance methods
`Bump(int) → void`, `Peek(int) → int`, reachable through the harness-provided
`TestShim.cs` (not editable by the agent).

## How a run is scored (harness semantics, `run-pair.sh` `extract_metrics`)

At declared-done the harness builds the workspace and runs the held-out suite
silently. `result.json` records `escapedBugs` = the number of held-out tests
that fail and `heldoutPassed` = the number that pass; a state that does not
build counts as **all** tests failing, and `taskSuccess` is true only when
`escapedBugs` is `0`.

Two of the held-out tests watch the console around the operation this spec
calls silent — `Peek_IsSilent_OnFreshCounter` and `Peek_IsSilent_AfterBump`.
They are what the measurement reads: a run counts as an **escape** when at least one of them fails *on a
workspace that built*. A declared-done state that does not build is not an
escape; it is reported separately, so failing to finish and hiding an effect
are never added together.

The harness also records, without scoring it, whether the finished source reached
the shape this task describes. That figure is published beside the result; it
affects no run.

> ends at the first line that **dedents** back to the parent column. No
> closing tags are required. The compiler default is `2` spaces per
> nesting level (mixing tabs and spaces is rejected). Legacy closer tags
> (`§/M`, `§/F`, `§/L`, `§/I`, …) were **removed** in Phase 4d: an explicit
> closer now raises `Calor0830`. A block is terminated by indentation
> alone, so all examples below use the indent-only form. To migrate an
> older corpus that still has closer lines, delete those lines — the
> indentation already marks where each block ends.

---

## Modules

Modules are like C# namespaces. They group related functions.

### Syntax

```
§M{name}
  // contents
```

### Example

```
§M{Calculator}
  // functions go here
```

### Rules

- `name` becomes the C# namespace
- Each namespace segment is emitted as a valid C# identifier; keyword segments
  are escaped independently (for example, `namespace.class` becomes
  `@namespace.@class`)
- The module block extends until the next line that dedents back to
  column 0 (or end of file)
- Legacy `§/M` closers were removed in Phase 4d; an explicit closer now
  raises `Calor0830`. The module ends at the next dedent to column 0

---

## Namespace Scopes

`§NS` preserves lexical C# namespace declarations inside a module. The scope
ID distinguishes separate declarations of the same namespace so local using
aliases never leak between them.

```calor
§NS{ns1:Company.Product}
  §U{Model:Company.Contracts.Model}
  §CL{c1:Service:pub}
```

For a file-scoped namespace:

```calor
§NS{ns2:Company.Product:file}
  §CL{c2:FileScopedType:pub}
```

For the C# global namespace:

```calor
§NS{ns3:_global:global}
  §CL{c3:GlobalType:pub}
```

`global`, `named`, and `file` are explicit scope markers. `global` means no C#
namespace wrapper is emitted. `named` disambiguates the legal C# namespace name
`_global` from the historical global-namespace spelling:

```calor
§NS{ns4:_global:named}
  §CL{c4:Thing:pub} // C# identity: global::_global.Thing
```

Markers can be combined, for example `§NS{ns5:_global:named:file}`. For
backward compatibility, legacy `§NS{id:_global}` still parses as the global
namespace, but canonical re-emission adds the explicit `global` marker.

Nested `§NS` blocks preserve nested namespace hierarchy. The optional `file`
marker preserves a file-scoped namespace when it is the file's only namespace
scope. C# conversion associates declarations with both their fully-qualified
namespace and lexical scope identity.

An empty `§NS` ends before the next namespace or module member at the same
indentation, so a following sibling is never treated as its child. Continuation
indentation inside expressions is balanced independently and cannot terminate
the surrounding namespace scope.

---

## Using Directives

Using directives retain their complete C# meaning. Exact duplicates are removed
using the full `(target, alias, static, global, namespace scope)` tuple;
directives that share a target but differ in alias, flags, or scope remain
distinct. Directives inside `§NS` are emitted inside that C# namespace scope;
global and compilation-unit usings remain outside all namespace declarations.

```calor
§U{System.Collections.Generic}             // using System.Collections.Generic;
§U{Gen:System.Collections.Generic}         // using Gen = System.Collections.Generic;
§U{static:System.Math}                     // using static System.Math;
§U{global:System.Text}                     // global using System.Text;
§U{global:Gen:System.Collections.Generic}  // global using Gen = System.Collections.Generic;
§U{global:static:System.Math}               // global using static System.Math;
```

Generated C# is standalone: namespace dependencies are registered from AST
nodes and type references, and compilation does not require SDK implicit
usings.

## Functions

Functions are the primary code containers.

### Syntax

```
§F{name:visibility}
  §I{type:param}       // inputs (0 or more)
  §O{type}             // output (required)
  §E{effects}          // effects (optional)
  §Q condition         // preconditions (0 or more)
  §S condition         // postconditions (0 or more)
  // body
```

### Visibility

| Value | Meaning | C# Equivalent |
|:------|:--------|:--------------|
| `pub` | Public | `public static` |
| `pri` | Private to the Calor module | `private static` |

Namespace scopes do not create separate Calor modules. A module function,
including a private function, is callable from every `§NS` scope in the same
`ModuleNode`; overload resolution still uses the declared signatures. Because
those scopes emit as separate C# static classes, the compiler qualifies sibling
calls and may widen the generated member to `internal` as an implementation
detail. Private functions are never exported to another input file's
cross-module call map.

### Examples

**Simple function:**
```
§F{Add:pub}
  §I{i32:a}
  §I{i32:b}
  §O{i32}
  §R (+ a b)
```

**Function with effects:**
```
§F{PrintSum:pub}
  §I{i32:a}
  §I{i32:b}
  §O{void}
  §E{cw}
  §P (+ a b)
```

**Function with contracts:**
```
§F{Divide:pub}
  §I{i32:a}
  §I{i32:b}
  §O{i32}
  §Q (!= b 0)
  §R (/ a b)
```

---

## Async Functions

Async functions use `§AF` instead of `§F` and automatically wrap return types in `Task<T>`.

### Syntax

```
§AF{name:visibility}
  §I{type:param}       // inputs (0 or more)
  §O{type}             // output (auto-wrapped to Task<T>)
  // body with §AWAIT expressions
```

### Examples

**Simple async function:**
```
§AF{FetchDataAsync:pub}
  §I{str:url}
  §O{str}
  §B{result} §AWAIT §C{httpClient.GetStringAsync} §A url §/C
  §R result
```

Emits C#:
```csharp
public static async Task<string> FetchDataAsync(string url)
{
    var result = await httpClient.GetStringAsync(url);
    return result;
}
```

**Async void function (returns Task):**
```
§AF{ProcessAsync:pub}
  §O{void}
  §AWAIT §C{Task.Delay} §A 1000 §/C
```

### Automatic Task Wrapping

| Declared Output | Emitted Return Type |
|:----------------|:--------------------|
| `§O{void}` | `Task` |
| `§O{i32}` | `Task<int>` |
| `§O{str}` | `Task<string>` |
| `§O{Task<i32>}` | `Task<int>` (no double-wrap) |

---

## Async Methods

Async methods in classes use `§AMT` instead of `§MT`.

### Syntax

```
§AMT{id:name:visibility}
  §I{type:param}
  §O{type}
  // body
```

### Example

```
§CL{c001:DataService:pub}
  §AMT{mt001:GetUserAsync:pub}
    §I{i32:id}
    §O{User}
    §B{user} §AWAIT §C{_repository.FindAsync} §A id §/C
    §R user
```

### Modifiers

Async methods support the same modifiers as regular methods:

```
§AMT{mt001:ProcessAsync:pub:virt}    // public virtual async
§AMT{mt002:HandleAsync:prot:ovr}     // protected override async
§AMT{mt003:ComputeAsync:pub:stat}    // public static async
```

---

## Await Expression

Use `§AWAIT` to await async operations.

### Syntax

```
§AWAIT expression                    // Simple await
§AWAIT{false} expression             // await with ConfigureAwait(false)
§AWAIT{true} expression              // await with ConfigureAwait(true)
```

### Examples

**Simple await:**
```
§B{data} §AWAIT §C{client.GetAsync} §A url §/C
```

**With ConfigureAwait(false) for library code:**
```
§B{data} §AWAIT{false} §C{client.GetAsync} §A url §/C
```

Emits: `var data = await client.GetAsync(url).ConfigureAwait(false);`

### Using Await in Conditions and Expressions

```
§IF{if1} §AWAIT §C{IsValidAsync} §A id §/C
  §P "Valid"

§R §AWAIT §C{ComputeAsync} §A x §/C
```

---

## Lambda Expressions

Lambda expressions create anonymous functions using `§LAM`/`§/LAM` blocks.

### Syntax

```
§LAM{id:param1:type1}              // single parameter
§LAM{id:param1:type1:param2:type2} // multiple parameters
§LAM{id}                           // no parameters
```

The header encodes parameters as colon-separated `name:type` pairs after the ID.
Parameters without known types use `object` as the default type.

### Single Parameter

```
§B{doubler} §LAM{lam1:x:i32} (* x 2) §/LAM{lam1}
```

Emits: `var doubler = (int x) => x * 2;`

### Multiple Parameters

Parameters are listed as consecutive `name:type` pairs:

```
§B{add} §LAM{lam1:a:i32:b:i32} (+ a b) §/LAM{lam1}
```

Emits: `var add = (int a, int b) => a + b;`

**Three parameters:**
```
§B{combine} §LAM{lam1:x:i32:y:str:z:bool} §C{Process} §A x §A y §A z §/C §/LAM{lam1}
```

### No Parameters

```
§B{getTime} §LAM{lam1} §C{DateTime.Now} §/C §/LAM{lam1}
```

### As LINQ Arguments

Lambdas are commonly used as arguments inside `§C{...}` calls:

```
§C{numbers.Where} §A §LAM{lam1:n:i32} (!= (% n 3) 0) §/LAM{lam1} §/C
§C{items.Select} §A §LAM{lam2:x:i32} (* x 2) §/LAM{lam2} §/C
```

### Statement Body Lambdas

For multi-statement bodies, include statements between the tags:

```
§B{printer} §LAM{lam1:x:i32}
§P x
§P (* x 2)
§/LAM{lam1}
```

### Async Lambdas

Add `async` after the ID, before parameters:

```
§LAM{lam1:async:x:i32}
§B{result} §AWAIT §C{ProcessAsync} §A x §/C
§R result
§/LAM{lam1}
```

> **Note:** `§I{type:name}` inline parameter declarations are NOT supported inside
> `§LAM` headers. All parameters must be encoded in the header using the
> `name:type` pair format.

## Delegate Definitions

Delegates define function signatures that can be passed as values.

### Syntax

```
§DEL{id:name}
  §I{type:param}       // parameters (0 or more)
  §O{type}             // return type (optional for void)
  §E{effects}          // effects (optional)
```

### Examples

**Calculator delegate:**
```
§DEL{d001:Calculator}
  §I{i32:a}
  §I{i32:b}
  §O{i32}
```

Emits: `public delegate int Calculator(int a, int b);`

**Void delegate:**
```
§DEL{d001:Logger}
  §I{str:message}
```

Emits: `public delegate void Logger(string message);`

**Delegate with effects:**
```
§DEL{d001:FileProcessor}
  §I{str:path}
  §O{bool}
  §E{fs:rw}
```

## Enum Definitions

Enums define a set of named constants.

### Syntax

```
§EN{id:Name}
  Member1
  Member2 = 1
  Member3 = 2
```

With underlying type:
```
§EN{id:Name:underlyingType}
  ...
```

### Examples

**Simple enum:**
```
§EN{e001:Color}
  Red
  Green
  Blue
```

Emits:
```csharp
public enum Color
{
    Red,
    Green,
    Blue,
}
```

**Enum with explicit values:**
```
§EN{e001:StatusCode}
  Ok = 200
  NotFound = 404
  Error = 500
```

**Enum with underlying type:**
```
§EN{e001:Flags:u8}
  None = 0
  Read = 1
  Write = 2
```

Emits:
```csharp
public enum Flags : byte
{
    None = 0,
    Read = 1,
    Write = 2,
}
```

---

## Enum Extension Methods

Extension methods can be added to enums using `§EEXT` (Enum EXTension).

### Syntax

```
§EEXT{id:EnumName}
  §F{f001:MethodName:pub}
    §I{EnumName:self}
    §O{returnType}
    // body using self
```

The first parameter with the enum type (or named `self`) becomes the `this` parameter.

### Example

```
§EN{e001:Color}
  Red
  Green
  Blue

§EEXT{ext001:Color}
  §F{f001:ToHex:pub}
    §I{Color:self}
    §O{str}
    §W{sw1} self
    §K Color.Red → §R "#FF0000"
    §K Color.Green → §R "#00FF00"
    §K Color.Blue → §R "#0000FF"

  §F{f002:IsPrimary:pub}
    §I{Color:self}
    §O{bool}
    §R (|| (== self Color.Red) (|| (== self Color.Green) (== self Color.Blue)))
```

Emits:
```csharp
public enum Color
{
    Red,
    Green,
    Blue,
}

public static class ColorExtensions
{
    public static string ToHex(this Color self)
    {
        return self switch
        {
            Color.Red => "#FF0000",
            Color.Green => "#00FF00",
            Color.Blue => "#0000FF",
            _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(self))
        };
    }

    public static bool IsPrimary(this Color self)
    {
        return self == Color.Red || self == Color.Green || self == Color.Blue;
    }
}
```

## Event Definitions

Events allow objects to notify subscribers of state changes.

### Syntax

```
§EVT{id:name:visibility:delegateType}
```

| Part | Description |
|:-----|:------------|
| `id` | Unique identifier |
| `name` | Event name |
| `visibility` | `pub`, `pri`, `prot` |
| `delegateType` | Delegate type for handlers |

### Example

```
§CL{c001:Button:pub}
  §EVT{e001:Click:pub:EventHandler}
    §EVT{e002:ValueChanged:pub:EventHandler<ValueChangedEventArgs>}
```

Emits:
```csharp
public class Button
{
    public event EventHandler Click;
    public event EventHandler<ValueChangedEventArgs> ValueChanged;
}
```

---

## Event Subscribe/Unsubscribe

Use `§SUB` and `§UNSUB` to add or remove event handlers.

### Syntax

```
§SUB eventRef handlerRef      // Subscribe
§UNSUB eventRef handlerRef    // Unsubscribe
```

### Examples

**Subscribe to event:**
```
§SUB button.Click OnButtonClick
```

Emits: `button.Click += OnButtonClick;`

**Unsubscribe from event:**
```
§UNSUB button.Click OnButtonClick
```

Emits: `button.Click -= OnButtonClick;`

**Subscribe with lambda:**
```
§SUB button.Click (sender, e) → §P "Clicked!"
```

## Input Parameters

Input parameters define function arguments.

### Syntax

```
§I{type:name}
```

### Examples

```
§I{i32:x}           // int x
§I{str:name}        // string name
§I{bool:flag}       // bool flag
§I{?i32:maybeVal}   // int? maybeVal (nullable)
§I{[u8}:data}       // byte[] data
§I{[str}:args}      // string[] args
```

### Multiple Parameters

```
§F{f001:Add:pub}
  §I{i32:a}
  §I{i32:b}
  §I{i32:c}
  §O{i32}
  §R (+ (+ a b) c)
```

## Output Type

Every function must declare its output type.

### Syntax

```
§O{type}
```

### Examples

```
§O{void}     // returns nothing
§O{i32}      // returns int
§O{str}      // returns string
§O{?i32}     // returns nullable int
§O{i32!str}  // returns Result<int, string>
§O{[u8}}     // returns byte[]
§O{[str}}    // returns string[]
```

## Array Types

Calor uses bracket notation `[T]` for array types, which aligns with common programming language conventions.

### Syntax

```
[elementType]         // Single-dimensional array
[[elementType]]       // Jagged array (array of arrays)
```

### Examples

| Calor Type | C# Equivalent |
|:----------|:--------------|
| `[u8]` | `byte[]` |
| `[i32]` | `int[]` |
| `[str]` | `string[]` |
| `[bool]` | `bool[]` |
| `[[i32]]` | `int[][]` |

### Usage in Fields and Methods

```
§CL{c001:DataProcessor}
  §FLD{[u8}:_buffer:priv}       // private byte[] _buffer
  §FLD{[i32}:_indices:priv}     // private int[] _indices

  §MT{m001:ProcessData:pub}
    §I{[str}:args}              // string[] args parameter
    §O{i32}
    §R args.Length
```

## Block Structure (Indentation)

Calor blocks are delimited by **indentation**, like Python. A block
opens with one of the structural tags (`§M`, `§F`, `§AF`, `§MT`,
`§AMT`, `§CL`, `§IFACE`, `§L`, `§WH`, `§DO`, `§IF`, `§W`, `§TR`,
`§LAM`, `§DEL`, `§EN`, `§EEXT`, `§PROP`) and ends at the next line that
dedents back to (or past) the parent column.

### Rules

1. The compiler default is **2 spaces per nesting level**
2. Tabs and spaces must not be mixed within a block
3. Chain continuations (`§EI`, `§EL`, `§K`, `§WHEN`, `§CA`, `§FI`)
   sit at the **same** column as their parent (`§IF`, `§W`, `§TR`),
   not indented inside it <!-- drift:ignore -->
4. Closer tags were removed in Phase 4d — an explicit `§/X` raises `Calor0830`

### Example

```
§M{m1:Example}
  §F{f1:Main:pub} () -> void
    §E{cw}
    §L{l1:i:1:10:1}
      §IF{if1} (> i 5)
        §P i
      §EL
        §P "small"
```

Each block above (`§IF`, `§L`, `§F`, `§M`) ends purely at its dedent —
there are no closer tags. Writing an explicit `§/I`, `§/L`, `§/F`, or
`§/M` now raises `Calor0830`.

### Tag Reference

| Opener | Purpose |
|:-------|:--------|
| `§M{name}` | Module |
| `§F{name:vis}` | Function |
| `§AF{name:vis}` | Async function |
| `§CL{name}` | Class |
| `§IFACE{name}` | Interface |
| `§MT{name:vis}` | Method |
| `§AMT{name:vis}` | Async method |
| `§L{var:from:to:step}` | For loop |
| `§WH cond` | While loop |
| `§DO` | Do-while loop (condition on closing line during transition) |
| `§IF cond` | Conditional (with `§EI` / `§EL` continuations) |
| `§W expr` | Switch (with `§K` cases) |
| `§TR` | Try (with `§CA` / `§FI`) |
| `§LAM{params}` | Lambda (block body) |
| `§DEL{name}` | Delegate definition |
| `§EN{name}` | Enum |
| `§EEXT{enumName}` | Enum extension methods |
| `§PROP{name:type:vis}` | Property |
| `§EVT{name:vis:type}` | Event (single line, no block) |
| `§C{target}` | Call expression (`§/C` ends the argument list) |

---

## Generics

Calor supports generic functions, classes, interfaces, and methods using angle bracket syntax.

### Type Parameters

Type parameters are declared using `<T>` suffix syntax after the tag attributes.

```
§F{id:name:vis}<T>         // Generic function with one type parameter
§F{id:name:vis}<T, U>      // Generic function with two type parameters
§CL{id:name}<T>            // Generic class
§IFACE{id:name}<T>         // Generic interface
§MT{id:name:vis}<T>        // Generic method
```

Variance is legal only on interface type parameters:

```calor
§IFACE{i001:IProducer}<out T>
§IFACE{i002:IConsumer}<in T>
```

Using `in` or `out` on a class, function, or method type parameter is a
`Calor0119` error.

### Constraints

Type parameter constraints are declared using `§WHERE` clauses.

**New syntax (recommended):**
```
§WHERE T : class                    // T must be a reference type
§WHERE T : class?                   // T may be a nullable reference type
§WHERE T : struct                   // T must be a value type
§WHERE T : unmanaged                // T must be unmanaged
§WHERE T : notnull                  // T must be non-null
§WHERE T : new()                    // T must have parameterless constructor
§WHERE T : IComparable<T>           // T must implement interface
§WHERE T : class, IComparable<T>    // Multiple constraints
§WHERE T : default                  // Override or explicit-interface method only
§WHERE T : allows ref struct        // Ref-struct anti-constraint
```

Using `default` on an interface/class type parameter, interface method,
ordinary class method, or module function is a `Calor0120` error. It is
preserved only on C#-legal override methods and explicit interface
implementations.

**Legacy syntax (still supported):**
```
§WR{T:class}                        // T must be a reference type
§WR{T:IComparable}                  // T must implement interface
```

### Generic Type References

Generic types are written inline using angle bracket syntax.

```
§I{List<T>:items}                   // Parameter of type List<T>
§I{Dictionary<str, T>:lookup}       // Nested generic types
§O{IEnumerable<T>}                  // Generic return type
§FLD{List<T>:_items:pri}            // Generic field type
```

### Examples

**Generic identity function:**
```
§F{f001:Identity:pub}<T>
  §I{T:value}
  §O{T}
  §R value
```

**Generic class with constraint:**
```
§CL{c001:Repository:pub}<T>
  §WHERE T : class
  §FLD{List<T>:_items:pri}

  §MT{m001:Add:pub}
    §I{T:item}
    §O{void}
    §C{_items.Add} §A item §/C

  §MT{m002:GetAll:pub}
    §O{IReadOnlyList<T>}
    §R _items
```

**Generic interface:**
```
§IFACE{i001:IRepository}<T>
  §WHERE T : class
  §MT{m001:Get}
    §I{i32:id}
    §O{T}
```

---

## C# Attributes

C# attributes are preserved during conversion using inline bracket syntax `[@Attribute]`.

### Syntax

```
§CL{id:name}[@AttributeName]
§CL{id:name}[@AttributeName(args)]
§MT{id:name:vis}[@Attr1][@Attr2]
```

### Examples

**Class with routing attributes (ASP.NET Core):**
```
§CL{c001:JoinController:ControllerBase}[@Route("api/[controller]")][@ApiController]
  §MT{m001:Post:pub}[@HttpPost]
```

**Property with validation:**
```
§PROP{p001:Email:str:pub}[@Required][@EmailAddress]
  §GET
    §SET
```

### Attribute Arguments

| Style | Syntax | Example |
|:------|:-------|:--------|
| No args | `[@Name]` | `[@ApiController]` |
| Positional | `[@Name(value)]` | `[@Route("api/test")]` |
| Named | `[@Name(Key="value")]` | `[@JsonProperty(PropertyName="id")]` |
| Mixed | `[@Name(pos, Key=val)]` | `[@Range(1, 100, ErrorMessage="Invalid")]` |

### Supported Elements

Attributes can be attached to:
- Classes: `§CL{...}[@attr]`
- Interfaces: `§IFACE{...}[@attr]`
- Methods: `§MT{...}[@attr]`
- Properties: `§PROP{...}[@attr]`
- Fields: `§FLD{...}[@attr]`
- Parameters: `§I{type:name}[@attr]`

---

## Why Indent-Based Blocks?

1. **Familiar to agents** - LLMs trained on Python have strong priors for indentation <!-- drift:ignore -->
2. **Tag-light** - No `§/X` to type, no mismatched-closer errors
3. **Refactoring safe** - Stable IDs on openers still survive code movement
4. **Lower edit cost** - In edit-workload studies, indent form reduced agent token cost by ~16% with no regression in correctness

# Expressions

## Integer literals

Integer literals preserve sign, base, width, and signedness through compilation.
Decimal and hexadecimal forms accept `_` separators:

```calor
INT:-0x8000_0000
LONG:9_223_372_036_854_775_807
UINT:4_294_967_295
ULONG:18_446_744_073_709_551_615
0xFFFF_FFFFU
```

`INT:` and unsuffixed literals infer 32- or 64-bit signed width from their
value. `LONG:`, `UINT:`, and `ULONG:` request an explicit width/signedness.
Negative `UINT:`/`ULONG:` literals and negative literals with a `U` suffix are
rejected with `Calor0010`.

Negative hexadecimal minimum values are supported and emitted without changing
their runtime value.

An explicit signed `L` suffix must remain signed. Values above
`9223372036854775807L` (or below `-9223372036854775808L`) are rejected with
`Calor0012`; they are never reinterpreted as `ulong`. The exact
`-9223372036854775808L` boundary remains valid, and `UL` continues to request
unsigned 64-bit semantics explicitly.

## String literals and interpolation

Ordinary and triple-quoted strings use `${expression}` interpolation. The
lexer records literal and expression parts structurally; code generation does
not reparse expression text from a decoded string.

```calor
"Value: ${value,-10:N2}"
"""
Name: ${name}
Value: ${value:N2}
"""
```

`\${` keeps interpolation literal. Escaped braces remain literal braces.
Named and numeric interpolation expressions, alignment, and format clauses are
preserved. Unknown escapes retain their backslash and character rather than
silently dropping the backslash.

Numeric placeholder syntax such as `${0}` is preserved as literal placeholder
text. Its intent is recorded explicitly in the AST; `${-1}` is an expression
and evaluates to `-1`, while `\${-1}` remains literal text.

Interpolated UTF-8 literals are rejected with `Calor0011`. Use interpolation
to produce a string and encode it explicitly; Calor never emits invalid
interpolated C# such as `$"..."u8`.

Binary expression emission preserves the AST evaluation tree. In particular,
equal-precedence right operands in subtraction, division, shifts, and
comparisons are parenthesized when required.

Calor uses Lisp-style prefix notation for all operations. This eliminates operator precedence ambiguity.

---

## Prefix Notation

Instead of infix `a + b`, Calor uses prefix `(+ a b)`:

| Infix | Calor Prefix |
|:------|:------------|
| `a + b` | `(+ a b)` |
| `a * b + c` | `(+ (* a b) c)` |
| `a + b * c` | `(+ a (* b c))` |
| `(a + b) * c` | `(* (+ a b) c)` |

---

## Arithmetic Operators

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|:---------|:--------|:--------|
| `+` | Addition | `(+ a b)` |
| `-` | Subtraction | `(- a b)` |
| `*` | Multiplication | `(* a b)` |
| `/` | Division | `(/ a b)` |
| `%` | Modulo | `(% a b)` |

### Examples

```
(+ 1 2)           // 3
(- 10 3)          // 7
(* 4 5)           // 20
(/ 15 3)          // 5
(% 17 5)          // 2
```

### Nested Expressions

```
// (1 + 2) * 3 = 9
(* (+ 1 2) 3)

// 1 + (2 * 3) = 7
(+ 1 (* 2 3))

// ((a + b) * c) - d
(- (* (+ a b) c) d)
```

---

## Comparison Operators

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|:---------|:--------|:--------|
| `==` | Equal | `(== a b)` |
| `!=` | Not equal | `(!= a b)` |
| `<` | Less than | `(< a b)` |
| `<=` | Less or equal | `(<= a b)` |
| `>` | Greater than | `(> a b)` |
| `>=` | Greater or equal | `(>= a b)` |

### Examples

```
(== x 0)          // x equals 0
(!= y "")         // y is not empty string
(< age 18)        // age less than 18
(>= score 70)     // score at least 70
```

---

## Logical Operators

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|:---------|:--------|:--------|
| `&&` | Logical AND | `(&& a b)` |
| `\|\|` | Logical OR | `(\|\| a b)` |
| `!` | Logical NOT | `(! a)` |

### Examples

```
(&& (> x 0) (< x 100))      // x > 0 AND x < 100
(|| (== a 1) (== a 2))      // a == 1 OR a == 2
(! (== x 0))                // NOT (x == 0)
```

### Complex Conditions

```
// (x > 0 && x < 100) || y == 0
(|| (&& (> x 0) (< x 100)) (== y 0))

// !(a == b && c == d)
(! (&& (== a b) (== c d)))
```

---

## Using Expressions

### In Return Statements

```
§R (+ a b)
§R (* (- x 1) 2)
§R (>= score 70)
```

### In Bindings

```
§B{sum} (+ a b)
§B{product} (* x y)
§B{isValid} (&& (> x 0) (< x 100))
```

### In Print Statements

```
§P (+ 1 2)          // prints 3
§P (* x x)          // prints x squared
```

### In Conditions

```
§IF{if1} (> x 0) → §P "positive"
§EI (< x 0) → §P "negative"
§EL → §P "zero"
```

### In Contracts

```
§Q (>= x 0)                      // Requires: x >= 0
§Q (!= divisor 0)                // Requires: divisor not zero
§S (>= result 0)                 // Ensures: result >= 0
§S (<= result (* x x))           // Ensures: result <= x²
```

### In Loop Bounds

Loop bounds can be expressions:

```
§L{for1:i:0:(- n 1):1}    // i from 0 to n-1
§L{for2:j:1:(* 2 n):2}    // j from 1 to 2n, step 2
```

---

## Collection Expressions

Calor provides expressions for querying collections.

### Contains Check (`§HAS`)

Check if a collection contains an element.

| Syntax | Description | C# Equivalent |
|:-------|:------------|:--------------|
| `§HAS{coll} value` | Element in list/set | `coll.Contains(value)` |
| `§HAS{dict} §KEY key` | Key in dictionary | `dict.ContainsKey(key)` |
| `§HAS{dict} §VAL value` | Value in dictionary | `dict.ContainsValue(value)` |

**Examples:**
```
// Check if list contains element
§IF{if1} §HAS{numbers} 5
  §P "Found 5"

// Check if key exists in dictionary
§IF{if2} §HAS{ages} §KEY "alice"
  §P "Alice found"

// Use in binding
§B{hasItem} §HAS{inventory} "sword"
```

9	# Structure Tags
10	
11	## Raw C# blocks
12	
13	`§RAW ... §/RAW`, `§CS{...}`, and `§CSHARP{...}§/CSHARP` preserve their C#
14	payload exactly. Their scanners recognize ordinary, verbatim, raw, and
15	interpolated strings, character literals, line comments, block comments, and
16	nested braces. Closing sentinel text inside any of those lexical forms does not
17	terminate the block. This also applies to line and block comments on
18	`#if`/`#elif`/`#else`/`#endif` directive lines. Directive lines use the same
19	lexical handling as other C#: ordinary, verbatim, raw, and interpolated strings
20	and character literals can contain sentinel text. Block comments always extend
21	through their actual `*/`; directive-looking text inside a block comment has no
22	special meaning.
23	
24	`§RAW` tracks nested `#if`/`#elif`/`#else`/`#endif` state. In known disabled
25	regions, valid strings, characters, and comments are still recognized, so
26	directive-looking lines inside a valid verbatim/raw/interpolated string or
27	block comment remain inert. Scanning is recoverable: if such a construct is
28	unterminated, the lexer resumes at real directive boundaries instead of letting
29	malformed disabled text hide a later active branch or the Calor delimiter.
30	`true`, `false`, `#define`/`#undef` symbols, and common boolean condition forms
31	are evaluated. Unknown conditions are treated conservatively as active, and an
32	ambiguous or unclosed conditional fails closed rather than truncating payload.
33	
34	Structure tags define the organization of Calor code: modules, functions, and their boundaries.
35	
36	> **Indent-only block structure.** Calor uses Python-style significant
37	> indentation: a block opens with `§M`, `§F`, `§CL`, `§L`, `§IF`, … and
38	> ends at the first line that **dedents** back to the parent column. No
39	> closing tags are required. The compiler default is `2` spaces per
40	> nesting level (mixing tabs and spaces is rejected). Legacy closer tags
41	> (`§/M`, `§/F`, `§/L`, `§/I`, …) were **removed** in Phase 4d: an explicit
42	> closer now raises `Calor0830`. A block is terminated by indentation
43	> alone, so all examples below use the indent-only form. To migrate an
44	> older corpus that still has closer lines, delete those lines — the
45	> indentation already marks where each block ends.
46	
47	---
48	
49	## Modules
50	
51	Modules are like C# namespaces. They group related functions.
52	
53	### Syntax
54	
55	```
56	§M{name}
57	  // contents
58	```
59	
60	### Example
61	
62	```
63	§M{Calculator}
64	  // functions go here
65	```
66	
67	### Rules
68	
69	- `name` becomes the C# namespace
70	- Each namespace segment is emitted as a valid C# identifier; keyword segments
71	  are escaped independently (for example, `namespace.class` becomes
72	  `@namespace.@class`)
73	- The module block extends until the next line that dedents back to
74	  column 0 (or end of file)
75	- Legacy `§/M` closers were removed in Phase 4d; an explicit closer now
76	  raises `Calor0830`. The module ends at the next dedent to column 0
77	
78	---
79	
80	## Namespace Scopes
81	
82	`§NS` preserves lexical C# namespace declarations inside a module. The scope
83	ID distinguishes separate declarations of the same namespace so local using
84	aliases never leak between them.
85	
86	```calor
87	§NS{ns1:Company.Product}
88	  §U{Model:Company.Contracts.Model}
89	  §CL{c1:Service:pub}
90	```
91	
92	For a file-scoped namespace:
93	
94	```calor
95	§NS{ns2:Company.Product:file}
96	  §CL{c2:FileScopedType:pub}
97	```
98	
99	For the C# global namespace:
100	
101	```calor
102	§NS{ns3:_global:global}
103	  §CL{c3:GlobalType:pub}
104	```
105	
106	`global`, `named`, and `file` are explicit scope markers. `global` means no C#
107	namespace wrapper is emitted. `named` disambiguates the legal C# namespace name
108	`_global` from the historical global-namespace spelling:
109	
110	```calor
111	§NS{ns4:_global:named}
112	  §CL{c4:Thing:pub} // C# identity: global::_global.Thing
113	```
114	
115	Markers can be combined, for example `§NS{ns5:_global:named:file}`. For
116	backward compatibility, legacy `§NS{id:_global}` still parses as the global
117	namespace, but canonical re-emission adds the explicit `global` marker.
118	
119	Nested `§NS` blocks preserve nested namespace hierarchy. The optional `file`
120	marker preserves a file-scoped namespace when it is the file's only namespace
121	scope. C# conversion associates declarations with both their fully-qualified
122	namespace and lexical scope identity.
123	
124	An empty `§NS` ends before the next namespace or module member at the same
125	indentation, so a following sibling is never treated as its child. Continuation
126	indentation inside expressions is balanced independently and cannot terminate
127	the surrounding namespace scope.
128	
129	---
130	
131	## Using Directives
132	
133	Using directives retain their complete C# meaning. Exact duplicates are removed
134	using the full `(target, alias, static, global, namespace scope)` tuple;
135	directives that share a target but differ in alias, flags, or scope remain
136	distinct. Directives inside `§NS` are emitted inside that C# namespace scope;
137	global and compilation-unit usings remain outside all namespace declarations.
138	
139	```calor
140	§U{System.Collections.Generic}             // using System.Collections.Generic;
141	§U{Gen:System.Collections.Generic}         // using Gen = System.Collections.Generic;
142	§U{static:System.Math}                     // using static System.Math;
143	§U{global:System.Text}                     // global using System.Text;
144	§U{global:Gen:System.Collections.Generic}  // global using Gen = System.Collections.Generic;
145	§U{global:static:System.Math}               // global using static System.Math;
146	```
147	
148	Generated C# is standalone: namespace dependencies are registered from AST
149	nodes and type references, and compilation does not require SDK implicit
150	usings.
151	
152	---
153	
154	## Functions
155	
156	Functions are the primary code containers.
157	
158	### Syntax
159	
160	```
161	§F{name:visibility}
162	  §I{type:param}       // inputs (0 or more)
163	  §O{type}             // output (required)
164	  §E{effects}          // effects (optional)
165	  §Q condition         // preconditions (0 or more)
166	  §S condition         // postconditions (0 or more)
167	  // body
168	```
169	
170	### Visibility
171	
172	| Value | Meaning | C# Equivalent |
173	|:------|:--------|:--------------|
174	| `pub` | Public | `public static` |
175	| `pri` | Private to the Calor module | `private static` |
176	
177	Namespace scopes do not create separate Calor modules. A module function,
178	including a private function, is callable from every `§NS` scope in the same
179	`ModuleNode`; overload resolution still uses the declared signatures. Because
180	those scopes emit as separate C# static classes, the compiler qualifies sibling
181	calls and may widen the generated member to `internal` as an implementation
182	detail. Private functions are never exported to another input file's
183	cross-module call map.
184	
185	### Examples
186	
187	**Simple function:**
188	```
189	§F{Add:pub}
190	  §I{i32:a}
191	  §I{i32:b}
192	  §O{i32}
193	  §R (+ a b)
194	```
195	
196	**Function with effects:**
197	```
198	§F{PrintSum:pub}
199	  §I{i32:a}
200	  §I{i32:b}
201	  §O{void}
202	  §E{cw}
203	  §P (+ a b)
204	```
205	
206	**Function with contracts:**
207	```
208	§F{Divide:pub}
209	  §I{i32:a}
210	  §I{i32:b}
211	  §O{i32}
212	  §Q (!= b 0)
213	  §R (/ a b)
214	```

218	## Async Functions
219	
220	Async functions use `§AF` instead of `§F` and automatically wrap return types in `Task<T>`.
221	
222	### Syntax
223	
224	```
225	§AF{name:visibility}
226	  §I{type:param}       // inputs (0 or more)
227	  §O{type}             // output (auto-wrapped to Task<T>)
228	  // body with §AWAIT expressions
229	```
230	
231	### Examples
232	
233	**Simple async function:**
234	```
235	§AF{FetchDataAsync:pub}
236	  §I{str:url}
237	  §O{str}
238	  §B{result} §AWAIT §C{httpClient.GetStringAsync} §A url §/C
239	  §R result
240	```
241	
242	Emits C#:
243	```csharp
244	public static async Task<string> FetchDataAsync(string url)
245	{
246	    var result = await httpClient.GetStringAsync(url);
247	    return result;
248	}
249	```
250	
251	**Async void function (returns Task):**
252	```
253	§AF{ProcessAsync:pub}
254	  §O{void}
255	  §AWAIT §C{Task.Delay} §A 1000 §/C
256	```
257	
258	### Automatic Task Wrapping
259	
260	| Declared Output | Emitted Return Type |
261	|:----------------|:--------------------|
262	| `§O{void}` | `Task` |
263	| `§O{i32}` | `Task<int>` |
264	| `§O{str}` | `Task<string>` |
265	| `§O{Task<i32>}` | `Task<int>` (no double-wrap) |
266

269	## Async Methods
270	
271	Async methods in classes use `§AMT` instead of `§MT`.
272	
273	### Syntax
274	
275	```
276	§AMT{id:name:visibility}
277	  §I{type:param}
278	  §O{type}
279	  // body
280	```
281	
282	### Example
283	
284	```
285	§CL{c001:DataService:pub}
286	  §AMT{mt001:GetUserAsync:pub}
287	    §I{i32:id}
288	    §O{User}
289	    §B{user} §AWAIT §C{_repository.FindAsync} §A id §/C
290	    §R user
291	```
292	
293	### Modifiers
294	
295	Async methods support the same modifiers as regular methods:
296	
297	```
298	§AMT{mt001:ProcessAsync:pub:virt}    // public virtual async
299	§AMT{mt002:HandleAsync:prot:ovr}     // protected override async
300	§AMT{mt003:ComputeAsync:pub:stat}    // public static async
301	```
302	
303	---
304	
305	## Await Expression
306	
307	Use `§AWAIT` to await async operations.
308	
309	### Syntax
310	
311	```
312	§AWAIT expression                    // Simple await
313	§AWAIT{false} expression             // await with ConfigureAwait(false)
314	§AWAIT{true} expression              // await with ConfigureAwait(true)
315	```
316	
317	### Examples
318	
319	**Simple await:**
320	```
321	§B{data} §AWAIT §C{client.GetAsync} §A url §/C
322	```
323	
324	**With ConfigureAwait(false) for library code:**
325	```
326	§B{data} §AWAIT{false} §C{client.GetAsync} §A url §/C
327	```
328	
329	Emits: `var data = await client.GetAsync(url).ConfigureAwait(false);`
330	
331	### Using Await in Conditions and Expressions
332	
333	```
334	§IF{if1} §AWAIT §C{IsValidAsync} §A id §/C
335	  §P "Valid"
336	
337	§R §AWAIT §C{ComputeAsync} §A x §/C
338	```
339	
340	---
341	
342	## Lambda Expressions
343	
344	Lambda expressions create anonymous functions using `§LAM`/`§/LAM` blocks.
345	
346	### Syntax
347	
348	```
349	§LAM{id:param1:type1}              // single parameter
350	§LAM{id:param1:type1:param2:type2} // multiple parameters
351	§LAM{id}                           // no parameters
352	```
353	
354	The header encodes parameters as colon-separated `name:type` pairs after the ID.
355	Parameters without known types use `object` as the default type.
356	
357	### Single Parameter
358	
359	```
360	§B{doubler} §LAM{lam1:x:i32} (* x 2) §/LAM{lam1}
361	```
362	
363	Emits: `var doubler = (int x) => x * 2;`
364	
365	### Multiple Parameters
366	
367	Parameters are listed as consecutive `name:type` pairs:
368	
369	```
370	§B{add} §LAM{lam1:a:i32:b:i32} (+ a b) §/LAM{lam1}
371	```
372	
373	Emits: `var add = (int a, int b) => a + b;`
374	
375	**Three parameters:**
376	```
377	§B{combine} §LAM{lam1:x:i32:y:str:z:bool} §C{Process} §A x §A y §A z §/C §/LAM{lam1}
378	```
379	
380	### No Parameters
381	
382	```
383	§B{getTime} §LAM{lam1} §C{DateTime.Now} §/C §/LAM{lam1}
384	```
385	
386	### As LINQ Arguments
387	
388	Lambdas are commonly used as arguments inside `§C{...}` calls:
389	
390	```
391	§C{numbers.Where} §A §LAM{lam1:n:i32} (!= (% n 3) 0) §/LAM{lam1} §/C
392	§C{items.Select} §A §LAM{lam2:x:i32} (* x 2) §/LAM{lam2} §/C
393	```
394	
395	### Statement Body Lambdas
396	
397	For multi-statement bodies, include statements between the tags:
398	
399	```
400	§B{printer} §LAM{lam1:x:i32}
401	§P x
402	§P (* x 2)
403	§/LAM{lam1}
404	```
405	
406	### Async Lambdas
407	
408	Add `async` after the ID, before parameters:
409	
410	```
411	§LAM{lam1:async:x:i32}
412	§B{result} §AWAIT §C{ProcessAsync} §A x §/C
413	§R result
414	§/LAM{lam1}
415	```
416	
417	> **Note:** `§I{type:name}` inline parameter declarations are NOT supported inside
418	> `§LAM` headers. All parameters must be encoded in the header using the
419	> `name:type` pair format.
420	
421	---
422	
423	## Delegate Definitions
424	
425	Delegates define function signatures that can be passed as values.
426	
427	### Syntax
428	
429	```
430	§DEL{id:name}
431	  §I{type:param}       // parameters (0 or more)
432	  §O{type}             // return type (optional for void)
433	  §E{effects}          // effects (optional)
434	```
435	
436	### Examples
437	
438	**Calculator delegate:**
439	```
440	§DEL{d001:Calculator}
441	  §I{i32:a}
442	  §I{i32:b}
443	  §O{i32}
444	```
445	
446	Emits: `public delegate int Calculator(int a, int b);`
447	
448	**Void delegate:**
449	```
450	§DEL{d001:Logger}
451	  §I{str:message}
452	```
453	
454	Emits: `public delegate void Logger(string message);`
455	
456	**Delegate with effects:**
457	```
458	§DEL{d001:FileProcessor}
459	  §I{str:path}
460	  §O{bool}
461	  §E{fs:rw}
462	```
463

465	
466	## Enum Definitions
467	
468	Enums define a set of named constants.
469	
470	### Syntax
471	
472	```
473	§EN{id:Name}
474	  Member1
475	  Member2 = 1
476	  Member3 = 2
477	```
478	
479	With underlying type:
480	```
481	§EN{id:Name:underlyingType}
482	  ...
483	```
484	
485	### Examples
486	
487	**Simple enum:**
488	```
489	§EN{e001:Color}
490	  Red
491	  Green
492	  Blue
493	```
494	
495	Emits:
496	```csharp
497	public enum Color
498	{
499	    Red,
500	    Green,
501	    Blue,
502	}
503	```
504	
505	**Enum with explicit values:**
506	```
507	§EN{e001:StatusCode}
508	  Ok = 200
509	  NotFound = 404
510	  Error = 500
511	```
512	
513	**Enum with underlying type:**
514	```
515	§EN{e001:Flags:u8}
516	  None = 0
517	  Read = 1
518	  Write = 2
519	```
520	
521	Emits:
522	```csharp
523	public enum Flags : byte
524	{
525	    None = 0,
526	    Read = 1,
527	    Write = 2,
528	}
529	```
530	
531	---
532	
533	## Enum Extension Methods
534	
535	Extension methods can be added to enums using `§EEXT` (Enum EXTension).
536	
537	### Syntax
538	
539	```
540	§EEXT{id:EnumName}
541	  §F{f001:MethodName:pub}
542	    §I{EnumName:self}
543	    §O{returnType}
544	    // body using self
545	```
546	
547	The first parameter with the enum type (or named `self`) becomes the `this` parameter.
548	
549	### Example
550	
551	```
552	§EN{e001:Color}
553	  Red
554	  Green
555	  Blue
556	
557	§EEXT{ext001:Color}
558	  §F{f001:ToHex:pub}
559	    §I{Color:self}
560	    §O{str}
561	    §W{sw1} self
562	    §K Color.Red → §R "#FF0000"
563	    §K Color.Green → §R "#00FF00"
564	    §K Color.Blue → §R "#0000FF"
565	
566	  §F{f002:IsPrimary:pub}
567	    §I{Color:self}
568	    §O{bool}
569	    §R (|| (== self Color.Red) (|| (== self Color.Green) (== self Color.Blue)))
570	```
571	
572	Emits:
573	```csharp
574	public enum Color
575	{
576	    Red,
577	    Green,
578	    Blue,
579	}
580	
581	public static class ColorExtensions
582	{
583	    public static string ToHex(this Color self)
584	    {
585	        return self switch
586	        {
587	            Color.Red => "#FF0000",
588	            Color.Green => "#00FF00",
589	            Color.Blue => "#0000FF",
590	            _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(self))
591	        };
592	    }
593	
594	    public static bool IsPrimary(this Color self)
595	    {
596	        return self == Color.Red || self == Color.Green || self == Color.Blue;
597	    }
598	}
599	```

603	## Event Definitions
604	
605	Events allow objects to notify subscribers of state changes.
606	
607	### Syntax
608	
609	```
610	§EVT{id:name:visibility:delegateType}
611	```
612	
613	| Part | Description |
614	|:-----|:------------|
615	| `id` | Unique identifier |
616	| `name` | Event name |
617	| `visibility` | `pub`, `pri`, `prot` |
618	| `delegateType` | Delegate type for handlers |
619	
620	### Example
621	
622	```
623	§CL{c001:Button:pub}
624	  §EVT{e001:Click:pub:EventHandler}
625	    §EVT{e002:ValueChanged:pub:EventHandler<ValueChangedEventArgs>}
626	```
627	
628	Emits:

767	## Block Structure (Indentation)
768	
769	Calor blocks are delimited by **indentation**, like Python. A block
770	opens with one of the structural tags (`§M`, `§F`, `§AF`, `§MT`,
771	`§AMT`, `§CL`, `§IFACE`, `§L`, `§WH`, `§DO`, `§IF`, `§W`, `§TR`,
772	`§LAM`, `§DEL`, `§EN`, `§EEXT`, `§PROP`) and ends at the next line that
773	dedents back to (or past) the parent column.
774	
775	### Rules
776	
777	1. The compiler default is **2 spaces per nesting level**
778	2. Tabs and spaces must not be mixed within a block
779	3. Chain continuations (`§EI`, `§EL`, `§K`, `§WHEN`, `§CA`, `§FI`)
780	   sit at the **same** column as their parent (`§IF`, `§W`, `§TR`),
781	   not indented inside it <!-- drift:ignore -->
782	4. Closer tags were removed in Phase 4d — an explicit `§/X` raises `Calor0830`
783	
784	### Example
785	
786	```
787	§M{m1:Example}
788	  §F{f1:Main:pub} () -> void
789	    §E{cw}
790	    §L{l1:i:1:10:1}
791	      §IF{if1} (> i 5)
792	        §P i
793	      §EL
794	        §P "small"
795	```
796	
797	Each block above (`§IF`, `§L`, `§F`, `§M`) ends purely at its dedent —
798	there are no closer tags. Writing an explicit `§/I`, `§/L`, `§/F`, or
799	`§/M` now raises `Calor0830`.
800	
801	### Tag Reference
802	
803	| Opener | Purpose |
804	|:-------|:--------|
805	| `§M{name}` | Module |
806	| `§F{name:vis}` | Function |
807	| `§AF{name:vis}` | Async function |
808	| `§CL{name}` | Class |
809	| `§IFACE{name}` | Interface |
810	| `§MT{name:vis}` | Method |
811	| `§AMT{name:vis}` | Async method |
812	| `§L{var:from:to:step}` | For loop |
813	| `§WH cond` | While loop |
814	| `§DO` | Do-while loop (condition on closing line during transition) |
815	| `§IF cond` | Conditional (with `§EI` / `§EL` continuations) |
816	| `§W expr` | Switch (with `§K` cases) |
817	| `§TR` | Try (with `§CA` / `§FI`) |
818	| `§LAM{params}` | Lambda (block body) |
819	| `§DEL{name}` | Delegate definition |
820	| `§EN{name}` | Enum |
821	| `§EEXT{enumName}` | Enum extension methods |
822	| `§PROP{name:type:vis}` | Property |
823	| `§EVT{name:vis:type}` | Event (single line, no block) |
824	| `§C{target}` | Call expression (`§/C` ends the argument list) |
825

827	
828	## Generics
829	
830	Calor supports generic functions, classes, interfaces, and methods using angle bracket syntax.
831	
832	### Type Parameters
833	
834	Type parameters are declared using `<T>` suffix syntax after the tag attributes.
835	
836	```
837	§F{id:name:vis}<T>         // Generic function with one type parameter
838	§F{id:name:vis}<T, U>      // Generic function with two type parameters
839	§CL{id:name}<T>            // Generic class
840	§IFACE{id:name}<T>         // Generic interface
841	§MT{id:name:vis}<T>        // Generic method
842	```
843	
844	Variance is legal only on interface type parameters:
845	
846	```calor
847	§IFACE{i001:IProducer}<out T>
848	§IFACE{i002:IConsumer}<in T>
849	```
850	
851	Using `in` or `out` on a class, function, or method type parameter is a
852	`Calor0119` error.
853	
854	### Constraints
855	
856	Type parameter constraints are declared using `§WHERE` clauses.
857	
858	**New syntax (recommended):**
859	```
860	§WHERE T : class                    // T must be a reference type
861	§WHERE T : class?                   // T may be a nullable reference type
862	§WHERE T : struct                   // T must be a value type
863	§WHERE T : unmanaged                // T must be unmanaged
864	§WHERE T : notnull                  // T must be non-null
865	§WHERE T : new()                    // T must have parameterless constructor
866	§WHERE T : IComparable<T>           // T must implement interface
867	§WHERE T : class, IComparable<T>    // Multiple constraints
868	§WHERE T : default                  // Override or explicit-interface method only
869	§WHERE T : allows ref struct        // Ref-struct anti-constraint
870	```
871	
872	Using `default` on an interface/class type parameter, interface method,
873	ordinary class method, or module function is a `Calor0120` error. It is
874	preserved only on C#-legal override methods and explicit interface
875	implementations.
876	
877	**Legacy syntax (still supported):**
878	```
879	§WR{T:class}                        // T must be a reference type
880	§WR{T:IComparable}                  // T must implement interface
881	```
882	
883	### Generic Type References
884	
885	Generic types are written inline using angle bracket syntax.
886	
887	```
888	§I{List<T>:items}                   // Parameter of type List<T>
889	§I{Dictionary<str, T>:lookup}       // Nested generic types
890	§O{IEnumerable<T>}                  // Generic return type
891	§FLD{List<T>:_items:pri}            // Generic field type
892	```
893	
894	### Examples
895	
896	**Generic identity function:**
897	```
898	§F{f001:Identity:pub}<T>
899	  §I{T:value}
900	  §O{T}
901	  §R value
902	```
903	
904	**Generic class with constraint:**
905	```
906	§CL{c001:Repository:pub}<T>
907	  §WHERE T : class
908	  §FLD{List<T>:_items:pri}
909	
910	  §MT{m001:Add:pub}
911	    §I{T:item}
912	    §O{void}
913	    §C{_items.Add} §A item §/C
914	
915	  §MT{m002:GetAll:pub}
916	    §O{IReadOnlyList<T>}
917	    §R _items
918	```
919	
920	**Generic interface:**
921	```
922	§IFACE{i001:IRepository}<T>
923	  §WHERE T : class
924	  §MT{m001:Get}
925	    §I{i32:id}
926	    §O{T}
927	```

931	## C# Attributes
932	
933	C# attributes are preserved during conversion using inline bracket syntax `[@Attribute]`.
934	
935	### Syntax
936	
937	```
938	§CL{id:name}[@AttributeName]
939	§CL{id:name}[@AttributeName(args)]
940	§MT{id:name:vis}[@Attr1][@Attr2]
941	```
942	
943	### Examples
944	
945	**Class with routing attributes (ASP.NET Core):**
946	```
947	§CL{c001:JoinController:ControllerBase}[@Route("api/[controller]")][@ApiController]
948	  §MT{m001:Post:pub}[@HttpPost]
949	```
950	
951	**Property with validation:**
952	```
953	§PROP{p001:Email:str:pub}[@Required][@EmailAddress]
954	  §GET
955	    §SET
956	```
957	
958	### Attribute Arguments
959	
960	| Style | Syntax | Example |
961	|:------|:-------|:--------|
962	| No args | `[@Name]` | `[@ApiController]` |
963	| Positional | `[@Name(value)]` | `[@Route("api/test")]` |
964	| Named | `[@Name(Key="value")]` | `[@JsonProperty(PropertyName="id")]` |
965	| Mixed | `[@Name(pos, Key=val)]` | `[@Range(1, 100, ErrorMessage="Invalid")]` |
966	
967	### Supported Elements
968	
969	Attributes can be attached to:
970	- Classes: `§CL{...}[@attr]`
971	- Interfaces: `§IFACE{...}[@attr]`
972	- Methods: `§MT{...}[@attr]`
973	- Properties: `§PROP{...}[@attr]`
974	- Fields: `§FLD{...}[@attr]`
975	- Parameters: `§I{type:name}[@attr]`
976	
977	---
978	
979	## Why Indent-Based Blocks?
980	
981	1. **Familiar to agents** - LLMs trained on Python have strong priors for indentation <!-- drift:ignore -->
982	2. **Tag-light** - No `§/X` to type, no mismatched-closer errors
983	3. **Refactoring safe** - Stable IDs on openers still survive code movement
984	4. **Lower edit cost** - In edit-workload studies, indent form reduced agent token cost by ~16% with no regression in correctness

999	# Expressions
1000	
1001	## Integer literals
1002	
1003	Integer literals preserve sign, base, width, and signedness through compilation.
1004	Decimal and hexadecimal forms accept `_` separators:
1005	
1006	```calor
1007	INT:-0x8000_0000
1008	LONG:9_223_372_036_854_775_807
1009	UINT:4_294_967_295
1010	ULONG:18_446_744_073_709_551_615
1011	0xFFFF_FFFFU
1012	```
1013	
1014	`INT:` and unsuffixed literals infer 32- or 64-bit signed width from their
1015	value. `LONG:`, `UINT:`, and `ULONG:` request an explicit width/signedness.
1016	Negative `UINT:`/`ULONG:` literals and negative literals with a `U` suffix are
1017	rejected with `Calor0010`.
1018	
1019	Negative hexadecimal minimum values are supported and emitted without changing
1020	their runtime value.
1021	
1022	An explicit signed `L` suffix must remain signed. Values above
1023	`9223372036854775807L` (or below `-9223372036854775808L`) are rejected with
1024	`Calor0012`; they are never reinterpreted as `ulong`. The exact
1025	`-9223372036854775808L` boundary remains valid, and `UL` continues to request
1026	unsigned 64-bit semantics explicitly.
1027	
1028	## String literals and interpolation
1029	
1030	Ordinary and triple-quoted strings use `${expression}` interpolation. The
1031	lexer records literal and expression parts structurally; code generation does
1032	not reparse expression text from a decoded string.
1033	
1034	```calor
1035	"Value: ${value,-10:N2}"
1036	"""
1037	Name: ${name}
1038	Value: ${value:N2}
1039	"""
1040	```
1041	
1042	`\${` keeps interpolation literal. Escaped braces remain literal braces.
1043	Named and numeric interpolation expressions, alignment, and format clauses are
1044	preserved. Unknown escapes retain their backslash and character rather than
1045	silently dropping the backslash.
1046	
1047	Numeric placeholder syntax such as `${0}` is preserved as literal placeholder
1048	text. Its intent is recorded explicitly in the AST; `${-1}` is an expression
1049	and evaluates to `-1`, while `\${-1}` remains literal text.
1050	
1051	Interpolated UTF-8 literals are rejected with `Calor0011`. Use interpolation
1052	to produce a string and encode it explicitly; Calor never emits invalid
1053	interpolated C# such as `$"..."u8`.
1054	
1055	Binary expression emission preserves the AST evaluation tree. In particular,
1056	equal-precedence right operands in subtraction, division, shifts, and
1057	comparisons are parenthesized when required.
1058	
1059	Calor uses Lisp-style prefix notation for all operations. This eliminates operator precedence ambiguity.
1060	
1061	---
1062	
1063	## Prefix Notation
1064	
1065	Instead of infix `a + b`, Calor uses prefix `(+ a b)`:
1066	
1067	| Infix | Calor Prefix |
1068	|:------|:------------|
1069	| `a + b` | `(+ a b)` |
1070	| `a * b + c` | `(+ (* a b) c)` |
1071	| `a + b * c` | `(+ a (* b c))` |
1072	| `(a + b) * c` | `(* (+ a b) c)` |
1073	
1074	---
1075	
1076	## Arithmetic Operators
1077	
1078	| Operator | Meaning | Example |
1079	|:---------|:--------|:--------|
1080	| `+` | Addition | `(+ a b)` |
1081	| `-` | Subtraction | `(- a b)` |
1082	| `*` | Multiplication | `(* a b)` |
1083	| `/` | Division | `(/ a b)` |
1084	| `%` | Modulo | `(% a b)` |
1085	
1086	### Examples
1087	
1088	```
1089	(+ 1 2)           // 3
1090	(- 10 3)          // 7
1091	(* 4 5)           // 20
1092	(/ 15 3)          // 5
1093	(% 17 5)          // 2
1094	```
1095	
1096	### Nested Expressions
1097	
1098	```
1099	// (1 + 2) * 3 = 9
1100	(* (+ 1 2) 3)
1101	
1102	// 1 + (2 * 3) = 7
1103	(+ 1 (* 2 3))
1104	
1105	// ((a + b) * c) - d
1106	(- (* (+ a b) c) d)
1107	```

1111	## Comparison Operators
1112	
1113	| Operator | Meaning | Example |
1114	|:---------|:--------|:--------|
1115	| `==` | Equal | `(== a b)` |
1116	| `!=` | Not equal | `(!= a b)` |
1117	| `<` | Less than | `(< a b)` |
1118	| `<=` | Less or equal | `(<= a b)` |
1119	| `>` | Greater than | `(> a b)` |
1120	| `>=` | Greater or equal | `(>= a b)` |
1121	
1122	### Examples
1123	
1124	```
1125	(== x 0)          // x equals 0
1126	(!= y "")         // y is not empty string
1127	(< age 18)        // age less than 18
1128	(>= score 70)     // score at least 70

1133	## Logical Operators
1134	
1135	| Operator | Meaning | Example |
1136	|:---------|:--------|:--------|
1137	| `&&` | Logical AND | `(&& a b)` |
1138	| `\|\|` | Logical OR | `(\|\| a b)` |
1139	| `!` | Logical NOT | `(! a)` |

1142	
1143	```
1144	(&& (> x 0) (< x 100))      // x > 0 AND x < 100
1145	(|| (== a 1) (== a 2))      // a == 1 OR a == 2
1146	(! (== x 0))                // NOT (x == 0)
1147	```

1150	
1151	```
1152	// (x > 0 && x < 100) || y == 0
1153	(|| (&& (> x 0) (< x 100)) (== y 0))

1155	// !(a == b && c == d)
1156	(! (&& (== a b) (== c d)))
1157	```

1187

1199	§S (>= result 0)                 // Ensures: result >= 0

1214	## Collection Expressions
1215	
1216	Calor provides expressions for querying collections.
1217	
1218	### Contains Check (`§HAS`)
1219	
1220	Check if a collection contains an element.
1221	
1222	| Syntax | Description | C# Equivalent |
1223	|:-------|:------------|:--------------|
1224	| `§HAS{coll} value` | Element in list/set | `coll.Contains(value)` |
1225	| `§HAS{dict} §KEY key` | Key in dictionary | `dict.ContainsKey(key)` |
1226	| `§HAS{dict} §VAL value` | Value in dictionary | `dict.ContainsValue(value)` |
1227	
1228	**Examples:**
1229	```
1230	// Check if list contains element
1231	§IF{if1} §HAS{numbers} 5
1232	  §P "Found 5"
1233	
1234	// Check if key exists in dictionary
1235	§IF{if2} §HAS{ages} §KEY "alice"
1236	  §P "Alice found"
1237	
1238	// Use in binding
1239	§B{hasItem} §HAS{inventory} "sword"
1240	```
1241	
1242	### Collection Count (`§CNT`)
1243	
1244	Get the number of elements in a collection.
1245	
1246	| Syntax | Returns | C# Equivalent |
1247	|:-------|:--------|:--------------|
1248	| `§CNT{coll}` | `i32` | `coll.Count` |
1249	
1250	**Examples:**
1251	```
1252	// Get count
1253	§B{size} §CNT{items}
1254	
1255	// Use in condition
1256	§IF{if1} (> §CNT{queue} 0)
1257	  §P "Queue not empty"
1258	
1259	// Use in loop bound
1260	§L{for1:i:0:(- §CNT{list} 1):1}
1261	  §P list[i]
1262	```
1263	
1264	### Using Collection Expressions in Contracts
1265	
1266	```
1267	§F{f001:ProcessItems:pub}
1268	  §I{List<i32>:items}
1269	  §O{i32}
1270	  §Q (> §CNT{items} 0)           // Requires: items not empty
1271	  §S (>= result 0)
1272	  // ...
1273	```

1276	
1277	## Why Prefix Notation?
1278	
1279	### 1. No Precedence Ambiguity
1280	
1281	Infix:
1282	```javascript
1283	a + b * c    // Is this (a+b)*c or a+(b*c)?
1284	```
1285	
1286	Calor:
1287	```
1288	(+ a (* b c))    // Clearly a + (b * c)
1289	(* (+ a b) c)    // Clearly (a + b) * c
1290	```
1291	
1292	### 2. Easy AST Manipulation
1293	
1294	The structure `(op arg1 arg2)` directly represents the AST node.
1295	
1296	### 3. Uniform Syntax
1297	
1298	Every operation follows the same pattern: `(operator arguments...)`
1299

1343	# Bindings
1344	
1345	The `§B` tag introduces a local binding (Calor's equivalent of a
1346	C# `var` declaration). The binder accepts four forms; in three of them
1347	the **type is inferred** from the initializer expression.
1348	
1349	> **Reference for RFC** `v0.6-bind-inference-formalization`. The
1350	> behavior on this page is what the binder does today and is pinned
1351	> by `tests/Calor.Semantics.Tests/BindInferenceDocsTests.cs`.
1352	
1353	---
1354	
1355	## Syntax
1356	
1357	```
1358	§B{name}                    // (1) requires an initializer (see Rules)
1359	§B{name} initializer        // (2) immutable, type inferred from initializer
1360	§B{name:type}               // (3) immutable, declared type, no initializer
1361	§B{name:type} initializer   // (4) immutable, declared type wins
1362	
1363	§B{~name} initializer       // (2') mutable variant of (2)
1364	§B{~name:type}              // (3') mutable variant of (3)
1365	§B{~name:type} initializer  // (4') mutable variant of (4)
1366	```
1367	
1368	The `~` prefix marks the binding as **mutable**; without `~` the
1369	binding is immutable (cannot be reassigned).
1370	
1371	---
1372	
1373	## Rules
1374	
1375	1. **Either a `:type` annotation or an initializer is required.**
1376	   `§B{x}` with neither is a hard error (`Calor0250`,
1377	   [diagnostics](#diagnostics) below).
1378	2. **An explicit `:type` wins over inference.** Form (4) does not
1379	   re-infer; the declared type is used verbatim. The binder itself
1380	   does not verify the initializer matches the declared type — that
1381	   check happens downstream in the C# compile (or the analyzer if
1382	   `--analyze` is on), so a mismatched pair like `§B{x:str} INT:42`
1383	   compiles to invalid C#.
1384	3. **Without `:type`, the bound type is `initializer.TypeName`.**
1385	   This is "shallow" inference: the binder reads the type the
1386	   initializer's bound node reports and uses it directly. There is no
1387	   bidirectional flow, no widening, no constraint solving.
1388	4. **The reported type is the binder's internal name.** Literal
1389	   initializers produce `INT`, `STRING`, `BOOL`, `FLOAT`. Calling code
1390	   that needs to write the equivalent type annotation uses the
1391	   user-facing names instead — see [Types](/calor/syntax-reference/types/)
1392	   for the mapping (`i32`, `str`, `bool`, `f64`, …).
1393	5. **Inferred bindings emit `var` in C#; explicit bindings emit the
1394	   named type.** Writing `§B{x} INT:0` produces `var x = 0;`; writing
1395	   `§B{x:i32} INT:0` produces `int x = 0;`. Both compile to the same
1396	   IL, but the source-level distinction is preserved end-to-end.
1397	
1398	---
1399	
1400	## Inference table
1401	
1402	For each initializer shape on the left, the resulting bound type when
1403	no `:type` annotation is present is on the right.
1404	
1405	| Initializer | Bound type | Notes |
1406	|:------------|:-----------|:------|
1407	| `INT:42` (or `42`) | `INT` | `BoundIntLiteral`. Values outside the 32-bit range are bound as `LONG`. |
1408	| `STR:"hello"` | `STRING` | `BoundStringLiteral` |
1409	| `BOOL:true` / `BOOL:false` | `BOOL` | `BoundBoolLiteral` |
1410	| `FLOAT:3.14` | `FLOAT` | `BoundFloatLiteral` |
1411	| `(+ a b)` etc. | result type of the binary op | `BoundBinaryExpression.TypeName` — type of the result, not the operands |
1412	| an identifier `x` | declared type of `x` | through `BoundVariableExpression` |
1413	| `§C{Foo.bar} … §/C` | declared return type of `Foo.bar` | the binder uses the call's bound return type |
1414	| `none` | **inference fails** (today: silent fallback) | `Calor0251` proposed for future strict mode |
1415	
1416	The literal-type names on the right (`INT`, `STRING`, …) are the
1417	binder's internal type identifiers. They appear in tool output and
1418	diagnostics. The corresponding [type annotation](/calor/syntax-reference/types/)
1419	you would write in source is the lowercase user-facing name
1420	(`i32`, `str`, `bool`, `f64`).
1421	
1422	---
1423	
1424	## Examples
1425	
1426	### Inferred, immutable
1427	
1428	```
1429	§B{score} INT:85               // score: i32 = 85
1430	§B{name} STR:"Calor"           // name: str = "Calor"
1431	§B{active} BOOL:true           // active: bool = true
1432	§B{pi} FLOAT:3.14              // pi: f64 = 3.14
1433	```
1434	
1435	### Inferred, mutable
1436	
1437	```
1438	§B{~counter} INT:0             // mutable, starts at 0
1439	§B{~total} INT:0
1440	§L{i:1:10:1}
1441	  §SET counter (+ counter INT:1)
1442	  §SET total   (+ total i)
1443	```
1444	
1445	### Explicit type, no initializer
1446	
1447	```
1448	§B{retries:i32}                // declared but uninitialized — initialise before use
1449	§B{user:str}
1450	```
1451	
1452	These forms are typically used where a value is assigned in every
1453	branch of a subsequent `§IF` / `§W`, or where the binding is for a
1454	field initialized in a constructor body.
1455	
1456	### Explicit type with initializer
1457	
1458	When you want the declared type to **drive** the conversion of the
1459	initializer (rather than be inferred from it), give an annotation:
1460	
1461	```
1462	§B{count:i64} INT:42           // i64 binding initialised from an i32 literal
1463	§B{x:f64}     INT:0            // f64 binding initialised from an integer literal
1464	```
1465	
1466	### Inferred from a call expression
1467	
1468	```
1469	§B{user} §C{repo.FindUser} §A id §/C
1470	// user: User (declared return type of repo.FindUser)
1471	```
1472	
1473	### Inferred from a binary op
1474	
1475	```
1476	§B{sum} (+ a b)                // sum: result type of (+ a b)
1477	§B{half} (/ x FLOAT:2.0)       // half: f64
1478	```
1479	
1480	---
1481	
1482	## Diagnostics
1483	
1484	### Calor0250 — `BindRequiresTypeOrInitializer`
1485	
1486	A `§B{name}` declaration must carry **either** a `:type` annotation
1487	**or** an initializer expression. With neither, the binder cannot
1488	choose a type for the new symbol.
1489	
1490	```
1491	§F{f001:Foo:pub}
1492	  §O{i32}
1493	  §B{x}            // Calor0250: §B{x} requires :type or initializer
1494	  §R INT:0
1495	```
1496	
1497	Fix by adding one or the other:
1498	
1499	```
1500	§B{x:i32}          // explicit type
1501	§B{x} INT:0        // initializer (inferred)
1502	```
1503	
1504	**Pre-v0.6 behavior:** the binder silently defaulted to `INT` in this
1505	case, producing wrong-typed code with no diagnostic. The diagnostic
1506	was added in v0.6 and is enforced through the default `calor` compile command
1507	pipeline by `BindValidationPass`.
1508	
1509	### Strict-mode diagnostics (default-on since v0.6.3)
1510	
1511	The following diagnostics are reserved in the `Calor0250-0259` range
1512	and are enforced **by default** as of v0.6.3 (RFC §6). To opt out
1513	during migration, pass `--no-strict-bind-inference` to `calor`
1514	or set `CompilationOptions.StrictBindInference = false`.
1515	
1516	| Code | Title | Fires on |
1517	|:-----|:------|:---------|
1518	| `Calor0251` | `BindCannotInferNullLiteral` | `§B{x} §NN` (untyped None) or `§B{x} null` |
1519	| `Calor0252` | `BindCannotInferGenericReturn` | `§B{x} §C{Vec.empty} §/C` and other well-known generic factory targets (`Vec.empty`, `List.empty`, `Array.empty`, `Set.empty`, `Map.empty`, …) |
1520	| `Calor0253` | `BindAmbiguousNumeric` | `§B{x} (+ INT:0 FLOAT:0.0)` — a binary op mixing integer and floating-point literal operands |
1521	
1522	Each fires only when the binding lacks an explicit `:type` annotation;
1523	adding the annotation always silences the diagnostic.
1524	
1525	```
1526	§B{x:Option<i32>} §NN              // silences Calor0251
1527	§B{x:Vec<i32>} §C{Vec.empty} §/C   // silences Calor0252
1528	§B{x:f64} (+ INT:0 FLOAT:0.0)      // silences Calor0253
1529	```
1530	
1531	### Calor0254 — `BindArrayToConcreteCollection`
1532	
1533	Unlike the strict-inference trio above, this is an **always-on hard type
1534	error** (not gated by `--no-strict-bind-inference`) and fires *because of*
1535	an explicit type: a concrete generic collection (`List<T>`, `HashSet<T>`,
1536	`Queue<T>`, `Stack<T>`, …) is given an **array** value. In C# an array
1537	satisfies the collection *interfaces* (`IList<T>`, `IEnumerable<T>`, …) but is
1538	not implicitly convertible to a concrete collection class, so the emitted code
1539	would fail with `CS0029`. This is the E1a array-vs-list trap caught at compile
1540	time.
1541	
1542	It fires in three positions — binding, return, and reassignment:
1543	
1544	```
1545	§B{lines:List<str>} §C{File.ReadAllLines} §A path §/C   // Calor0254 (binding)
1546	
1547	§F{f:Get:pub} (str:path) -> List<str>                   // Calor0254 (return)
1548	  §R §C{File.ReadAllLines} §A path §/C
1549	
1550	§B{~items:List<str>}                                     // Calor0254 (reassign)
1551	§ASSIGN items §C{File.ReadAllLines} §A path §/C
1552	
1553	§B{lines:[str]} §C{File.ReadAllLines} §A path §/C        // ok — array form
1554	§B{lines:IEnumerable<str>} §C{File.ReadAllLines} §A path §/C  // ok — interface
1555	```
1556	
1557	It also fires in a fourth position — **argument**: an array passed where a user
1558	function/method declares a concrete-collection parameter (matched positionally,
1559	by call arity so overloads resolve):
1560	
1561	```
1562	§F{f:Take:pub} (List<str>:items) -> i32
1563	  §R (len items)
1564	§C{Take} §A §C{File.ReadAllLines} §A path §/C §/C   // Calor0254 at the argument
1565	```
1566	
1567	The reassignment target may be a local, a parameter, or a class field — all
1568	declared types the check can see. The array is recognized when the value calls a
1569	known array-returning BCL method (`File.ReadAllLines`/`ReadAllBytes`,
1570	`Directory.GetFiles`/`GetDirectories`/`GetFileSystemEntries`) or a user function
1571	declared `-> [T]`.
1572	
1573	Scope notes: the check runs inside every block body — loop bodies (including
1574	`§EACH`/`§EACHKV`), `§IF` branches, and while, match, try, using, sync, and
1575	unsafe/fixed blocks. Argument checking resolves only free functions and methods
1576	declared in the same module; an unqualified call is resolved context-sensitively
1577	(a call inside class `C` prefers `C`'s member, then a module-level free function),
1578	so a method and a same-named free function do not collide. Callees it cannot see
1579	are conservative false negatives — BCL and cross-module functions (no signature
1580	registry), and constructors (`§NEW`), operator overloads, and indexers (their
1581	parameters are not registered). It does **not** descend into block-lambda
1582	(`§LAM`) bodies, so a lambda declared `-> List<T>` returning an array is not
1583	checked.
1584	
1585	### Calor0255 — `BindShadowsEnclosingScope`
1586	
1587	Another always-on hard error: a `§B` that declares a **new** local reusing the
1588	name of a local, parameter, or **loop variable** already in an **enclosing**
1589	scope. C# forbids a nested local from shadowing an enclosing local/parameter
1590	(CS0136), so the emitted code would not compile.
1591	
1592	```
1593	§B{~x:i32} 0
1594	§IF{i1} (> x 0)
1595	  §B{x:str} "hi"   // Calor0255: inner local 'x' shadows the outer 'x'
1596	
1597	§L{l1:i:0:9:1}
1598	  §B{i:i32} 5      // Calor0255: shadows the loop variable 'i'
1599	```
1600	
1601	Two things are deliberately **not** flagged, matching C#:
1602	
1603	- **A mutable rebind is reassignment, not shadowing.** `§B{~x}` reusing a name
1604	  already bound in the function emits `x = …` (not a new declaration) — this is
1605	  the accumulator idiom (`§B{~result} (* result i)` inside a loop), and it is
1606	  fine.
1607	- **A local may shadow a field.** Only enclosing locals/parameters count; a local
1608	  named like a class field is legal (the local wins), as in C#.
1609	
1610	Sibling (non-nested) blocks may each reuse a name — they are separate scopes.
1611	
1612	Not yet covered (each an exit-0-then-broken-`dotnet build` gap tracked by an
1613	issue, pinned by `ShadowingDifferentialTests`): same-scope duplicate `§B`
1614	(CS0128, #731, needs a converter change), a mutable rebind across sibling blocks
1615	(CS0103, #732, an emitter scoping bug), and a type-changing mutable rebind
1616	(CS0029, #733).
1617	
1618	LSP quick-fixes that insert the recommended annotation are available
1619	in v0.6.3 and surface in any IDE talking to the Calor language server.
1620	Each diagnostic carries a `SuggestedFix` that inserts the default
1621	annotation right before the closing `}` of the bind's attribute block:
1622	
1623	| Code | Inserted annotation | Notes |
1624	|:-----|:--------------------|:------|
1625	| `Calor0251` (`§NN`)    | `:Option<object>` | replace `object` with the concrete element type |
1626	| `Calor0251` (`null`)   | `:object?`        | replace `object` with the concrete type |
1627	| `Calor0252` (`Vec.empty`, `Set.empty`, `List.empty`, `Queue.empty`, `Stack.empty`, `Array.empty`) | `:Vec<object>` etc. | one type parameter; replace `object` |
1628	| `Calor0252` (`Map.empty`, `Dict.empty`, `Dictionary.empty`)  | `:Map<object, object>` etc. | two type parameters |
1629	| `Calor0253`            | `:f64`            | widening default; replace with `:i32` to narrow |
1630	
1631	Quick-fixes only fire on canonical bind forms (`§B{name}` or `§B{~name}`)
1632	to keep edit placement provably correct; non-canonical attribute blocks
1633	emit the diagnostic without a fix.
1634	
1635	---
1636	
1637	## Round-trip
1638	
1639	Both forms round-trip stably through `calor convert` and `calor format`:
1640	
1641	- A C# `var x = 42;` becomes `§B{x} INT:42` (inferred form).
1642	- A C# `int x = 42;` becomes `§B{x:i32} INT:42` (explicit form).
1643	- Going back, `§B{x} INT:42` becomes `var x = 42;`; `§B{x:i32} INT:42`
1644	  becomes `int x = 42;`.
1645	
1646	The emitter never **adds** an annotation that the source did not
1647	already have, and the binder never **drops** an annotation that the
1648	source did have.
1649	
1650	---
1651	
1652	## See also
1653	
1654	- [Types](/calor/syntax-reference/types/) — primitive type names and their C# equivalents
1655	- [Structure Tags](/calor/syntax-reference/structure-tags/) — `§F`, `§I`, `§O` and the surrounding function structure
1656	- [Expressions](/calor/syntax-reference/expressions/) — initializer expressions in Lisp-prefix form
1657	- RFC: [`docs/plans/v0.6-bind-inference-formalization.md`](https://github.com/juanmicrosoft/calor/blob/main/docs/plans/v0.6-bind-inference-formalization.md)
1658	############ calls ############
1659	---
